resources.string: Inherited in the descent
In the attributes lesson, the type went down the tree as an inherited attribute. In recursive descent, each nonterminal becomes a function. See how the inherited attribute reaches it.
The synthesized attribute comes back in the return: function T gives back the type. The inherited one goes as a parameter: function L receives h. id matches the identifier and gives back its name.
With the input float a, b, which line puts b in the table? Tap it.
a comes right after the type, and b comes after the comma. Who matches the comma?
L puts a. b comes after the comma, and R is the one that matches the comma. h reached R as a parameter, through the call L made.
This is the trace of the calls. The same float goes from function to function, as a parameter, until it reaches each id.
A translation scheme is the grammar with actions in braces inside the rules. The action runs when the parser goes through that point of the rule.
The action passes T's type to L's inherited attribute. Where in the rule for D can it go? Tap it.
The action reads T's type. And L needs the inherited attribute ready when it starts.
Before T, the type doesn't exist yet. After L, a and b are already in the table with no type. Only between T and L does it work.

In function D, the action in the middle of the rule is the call to L with t. It runs after T and before L. The inherited attribute becomes a parameter, and the synthesized one becomes the return value.
Functions in the table
Up to now, the symbol table held variables. Now the program has functions. Each function opens its own table, a child of the global one.
Which table do the parameters a and b go into? Tap it.
Who can use a? Only the code inside soma.
Into soma's table, together with s. Outside soma, nobody sees a or b.
%1$s: %2$s, parameter
The function goes into the global table. The entry keeps the type it returns and the types of its parameters. The parameters go into the function's own table.
Inside main, someone writes x equals a. What does the lookup for a find? Tap it.
The a in soma's table
An a in the global table
Nothing: the compiler reports an error
The lookup leaves main and goes up to the parent. Is soma's table on that path?
From main, the lookup goes up to the global table, and there is no a there. soma's table is a sibling of main's table, not its parent. So the compiler reports an error.
In a call, the compiler looks the function up in the global table. Then it compares that entry with what the call sends. What the call sends are the arguments.
Which call does the compiler reject? Tap it.
Count the arguments and compare with soma's entry.
soma asks for two parameters, and this call sends only one argument. The count doesn't match.
That's why the function keeps its parameter types in the global table. Without that entry, the compiler would have nothing to compare the call with.
Array access
An array keeps its elements side by side in memory. Each int takes 4 bytes. That's why the addresses jump by 4.
Array v starts at address 1000. Where does the element with index 2 live? Tap it.
The index starts at zero. How many elements come before the one with index 2?
Two elements come before it, 4 bytes each. So 1000 plus 4 times 2 gives 1008.
In three-address code, the compiler first computes the offset. The offset is the distance, in bytes, from the start of the array to the element.
Why does the compiler multiply the index by 4? Tap it.
The array has 4 elements
Each int takes 4 bytes
The index counts by 4
Think about the size of each element, not the size of the array.
The 4 comes from the size of an int. In an array of a hundred elements, i would also be multiplied by 4.
In MIPS, la loads the address where the array starts. lw brings the value of i into a register.
Which line does i times 4? Tap it.
There is no mul here. Look for the line that moves the bits of i.
sll pushes the bits two places to the left. Each place doubles the number, so two places multiply by 4. And it costs less than mul.
add adds the start of the array and the offset. lw reads the word at that address. With i equal to 2, x ends up with 30.
To write into the array, the address math is the same. Only the end changes: an sw instead of the lw.
It's a digit, so it enters the if, and v starts at zero. The first turn of the while adds the four.
The loop stops. But the plus has already left the input: it was read one too many. ungetc puts it back.
Without ungetc
A common mistake is forgetting ungetc. See the same code without that line, reading another input: seven times thirteen.
Which tokens come out of this input, now without ungetc? Tap it.
The while stops because it read the times sign. Without ungetc, who puts it back?
The times sign was read to stop the while, and nobody put it back. It disappears, and the parser gets two numbers in a row.
